shared_authoritative_material.content:
SHARED SYNTHETIC ECONOMIC EVIDENCE CORPUS
All observations, contextual information and claims in this corpus are fictional and constructed for educational purposes. They must not be attributed to actual households, businesses, authorities or published economic research. Preserve observation pairs, units, sample definitions and contextual facts across independently generated components. Calculate Pearson correlation coefficients directly from the listed observations before publication, using unrounded values internally and reporting coefficients to two decimal places. Do not invent additional observations for these datasets.

DATASET A: Household income and expenditure
Ten fictional households observed during the same month. Each pair represents monthly disposable household income and monthly household consumption expenditure, both in pounds sterling. Observations: (1500,1350), (1800,1450), (2100,1800), (2400,1750), (2700,2150), (3000,2350), (3300,2400), (3600,2850), (3900,2700), (4200,3200). Household size, accumulated wealth, borrowing and employment circumstances are not recorded. The data describe a cross-sectional association and do not establish the effect of changing an individual household's income.

DATASET B: Product price and quantity sold
Eight fictional retailers selling the same type of product during one week. Each pair represents price per unit in pounds sterling and units sold during the week. Observations: (10,105), (12,96), (14,85), (16,78), (18,67), (20,58), (22,48), (24,40). Retailers differ in potentially relevant but unrecorded characteristics. These are observations across retailers, not observations from a controlled price experiment.

DATASET C: Temperature and household energy expenditure
Nine fictional monthly observations. Each pair represents average outdoor temperature in degrees Celsius and monthly household energy expenditure in pounds sterling. Observations: (0,180), (5,145), (10,120), (15,105), (20,100), (25,105), (30,120), (35,145), (40,180). The fictional household uses energy for heating and cooling. The symmetric observations produce a non-linear relationship with a Pearson correlation coefficient of exactly zero. This constructed pattern is not evidence of the actual response of household energy expenditure to temperature.

DATASET D: Advertising expenditure and sales revenue
Ten fictional small retailers in the same broad retail sector, observed during the same month. Each pair represents monthly advertising expenditure and monthly sales revenue, both in thousands of pounds sterling. Observations: (1,18), (2,21), (3,25), (4,27), (5,32), (6,35), (7,38), (8,42), (9,45), (10,15). Retailers are labelled R1 through R10 in the listed order. R10 is an unusual observation relative to the pattern of the other nine retailers. No explanation for R10's position is available in the initial evidence. Do not classify R10 as an error or remove it without justification.

RECURRING CASE D: Does advertising increase sales?
The fictional claim is: Increasing a retailer's advertising expenditure will increase its sales revenue. Dataset D is the initial evidence. Plausible mechanisms include advertising attracting customers, retailers with greater sales revenue having more resources available for advertising, and retailer size or market demand influencing both expenditure and revenue. These are hypotheses, not established facts about the observed retailers. The unusual observation does not by itself establish or disprove any of these mechanisms. Learners must distinguish the observed association from the causal claim.

CASE D SUPPLEMENT: Release only during E8 or later.
For R1 through R10 respectively, monthly sales revenue in the preceding month, in thousands of pounds, was 17, 20, 24, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 44 and 14. Advertising budgets for the observed month were set at the beginning of that month, after managers had access to preceding-month sales figures. There was no random allocation of advertising budgets. The dataset does not record retailer size, customer footfall, promotional discounts, advertising quality or managers' actual reasons for setting budgets. The supplementary evidence makes prior sales performance a particularly relevant alternative explanation for differences in advertising expenditure. It does not establish that prior sales determined advertising budgets, that advertising had no effect, or that the observed association is entirely attributable to reverse causality or confounding. The supplementary evidence provides no confirmed explanation for R10.

DATASET E: Vocational training participation and unemployment
Ten fictional local labour market areas observed during the same calendar year. Each pair represents the percentage of working-age residents participating in vocational training during that year and the annual average unemployment rate as a percentage of the labour force. Observations: (4,8.5), (5,7.8), (6,8.0), (7,6.9), (8,7.1), (9,6.2), (10,6.5), (11,5.4), (12,5.8), (13,4.9). The fictional policy claim is: Expanding vocational training participation will reduce local unemployment. Areas differ in industrial composition, labour demand, educational provision and public funding. These characteristics are not quantified. The timing of individual training participation relative to changes in employment status is not recorded. The evidence is observational and aggregated at area level; it does not track individual participants' employment outcomes. Plausible alternative explanations include stronger local economies supporting both training opportunities and employment, and local labour market conditions influencing decisions about training provision or participation. No alternative mechanism is established by the supplied evidence.

RELEASE AND REUSE RULES
E1 introduces Datasets A and B. E2 introduces Datasets C and D. E3 revisits Dataset A. E4 uses Datasets A and B and brief contrasting hypothetical mechanisms to establish general explanatory principles; it must not supply worked answers to Case D. E5 uses Dataset D and its initial case information only. E6 retrieves general concepts using compact examples without releasing new Case D evidence. E7 uses Dataset B to model the evidential value of temporal ordering and meaningful comparisons without inventing further observations or releasing the Case D supplement. E8 revisits Case D and releases its supplementary evidence. E9 introduces Dataset E and its policy claim for independent transfer. E10 revisits Dataset E for formative evaluation and refinement. Do not expose Dataset E or its worked interpretation before E9, or release worked evaluations of Dataset E before E10.

ACCESSIBILITY AND STATISTICAL INTEGRITY
Every scatterplot must be generated from its exact observation pairs and accompanied by an accessible data table with descriptive column headings, units and observation identifiers where applicable. Alternative representations used for independent interpretation must not disclose the intended analytical conclusions. Worked examples may explicitly explain patterns after the relevant learner response opportunity. Correlation coefficients must describe linear association only. Do not use universal numerical thresholds for strong or weak correlation, infer causal effects from the synthetic observations, or present plausible mechanisms as established case facts.

commissions.title: Reading relationships in economic data
commissions.specification_text:
Create a ten-minute explanatory learning experience for first-year undergraduate economics students who have basic mathematical knowledge and familiarity with descriptive statistics but no formal econometric training. The primary educational job is to establish a systematic approach to interpreting bivariate economic evidence. Introduce Datasets A and B from the shared authoritative material as first-pass unfamiliar evidence. Model how to identify the variables and their units, describe the direction and strength of association, recognise variability around a general pattern and interpret a supplied Pearson correlation coefficient. Connect each interpretation to specific features of the observations rather than relying on the coefficient alone. Contrast positive and negative relationships using household income and expenditure and retailer prices and quantities sold. Establish that describing an association does not explain why it exists. Include brief prediction or interpretation checks embedded within the explanation, followed by concise explanatory feedback. Address the misconception that a strong statistical relationship implies that one variable causes the other. Do not require manual calculation of correlation coefficients or introduce formal econometric methods. Provide accessible data tables equivalent to all scatterplots. Use the exact shared observations and verify derived coefficients. Label the evidence as synthetic. Allocate approximately six minutes to worked explanation, two minutes to interpretation checks and two minutes to feedback and consolidation. Do not require a persistent written response or declare a Journal producer.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Describe the direction, strength and variability of a bivariate economic relationship using graphical or equivalent tabular evidence.","related_concepts":["Bivariate data","Direction of association","Strength of association","Variability"],"cognitive_level":"apply"},{"statement":"Interpret the sign and magnitude of a supplied correlation coefficient as a description of linear association rather than evidence of causation.","related_concepts":["Pearson correlation coefficient","Linear association","Statistical interpretation"],"cognitive_level":"understand"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: This is the opening experience of a single two-week Learning Journey. Learners bring basic descriptive statistical knowledge but have not yet encountered the journey's approach to causal reasoning. Use the locked synthetic Datasets A and B. Dataset A concerns ten households' monthly disposable income and consumption expenditure; Dataset B concerns eight retailers' prices and weekly quantities sold. These are observational datasets, not controlled interventions. Establish terminology and interpretative conventions that later components can assume. Dataset A will be revisited in the distinction between association and causation, and Dataset B will support later consideration of evidence that could strengthen causal explanations. Do not introduce the later advertising or vocational training cases.

commissions.title: Interpreting contrasting statistical relationships
commissions.specification_text:
Create a ten-minute practice experience in which first-year undergraduate economics students apply their established approach to statistical interpretation to two unfamiliar synthetic datasets. Use Dataset C to expose the limitations of Pearson correlation for describing non-linear relationships and Dataset D to explore the influence of an unusual observation. Assume learners can already interpret the direction and strength of straightforward linear associations and the sign and magnitude of a supplied correlation coefficient. Begin with a concise interpretative framework covering variables, direction, strength, pattern and limitations. Ask learners to formulate their own descriptions before revealing worked interpretations. For Dataset C, require learners to reconcile the observed pattern with the zero correlation coefficient. For Dataset D, require learners to describe the overall association, identify the unusual observation and explain why the coefficient alone may provide an incomplete description. Declare elicitation_id E2 for one coherent learner-authored text response interpreting Dataset D. The response must be a genuine statistical interpretation, not a reflection on the learning process. Capture it as the persistent artefact comm_2.E2. The Dataset C interpretation may remain local to the activity. Provide worked responses and criterion-referenced feedback after learners have attempted the interpretations. Feedback must explain why zero linear correlation can coexist with a systematic non-linear relationship and why an unusual observation should not automatically be treated as erroneous or excluded. Use the locked observations and verified correlation coefficients, with equivalent accessible tables. Do not reveal explanations for the advertising and sales relationship or the supplementary Case D evidence. Allocate approximately two minutes to orientation, five minutes to interpretation and three minutes to feedback.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Explain how a non-linear economic relationship can coexist with a weak or zero Pearson correlation coefficient.","related_concepts":["Non-linear association","Pearson correlation","Limitations of correlation"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"},{"statement":"Construct a contextualised statistical interpretation that accounts for the overall pattern and an unusual observation without making unsupported causal claims.","related_concepts":["Outliers","Statistical interpretation","Observational evidence"],"cognitive_level":"apply"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_1 established how to interpret straightforward positive and negative relationships using household income and expenditure and retailer prices and quantities sold. Learners now encounter unfamiliar evidence that complicates this approach. Dataset C has a symmetric non-linear pattern and zero Pearson correlation. Dataset D concerns ten retailers' monthly advertising expenditure and sales revenue, with R10 unusual relative to the other nine observations. Preserve the exact shared observations and retailer identifiers. No confirmed explanation for R10 is available. Dataset D establishes the recurring advertising case that will be developed in comm_5 and revisited with supplementary evidence in comm_8. The learner-authored statistical interpretation comm_2.E2 will be included in the Learning Journal and may be displayed read-only in comm_5 to support continuity between description and explanation.

commissions.title: Distinguishing association from causation
commissions.specification_text:
Create an eight-minute conceptual discrimination practice experience for first-year undergraduate economics students. Learners have already interpreted positive, negative and non-linear statistical relationships and considered the limitations of correlation coefficients. Revisit familiar Dataset A rather than introducing a new evidence set. Establish through a brief modelled contrast the difference between a statement describing an observed association, a statement proposing a possible causal explanation and a statement asserting a causal effect. Ask learners to classify contrasting statements about household income and consumption expenditure and identify the reasoning or language that distinguishes them. Include opportunities to recognise and improve statements that make stronger causal claims than the evidence warrants. The principal activity should be intellectual discrimination and justification rather than passive reading or memorisation of definitions. Use concise selected-response reasoning checks and explanatory feedback to address why a strong association does not establish what would happen if an individual household's income changed. Explain that causal claims are not necessarily false merely because the available evidence is insufficient to establish them. Preserve the shared dataset facts and distinguish hypothetical mechanisms from observed evidence. Provide accessible representations of any reused graphical evidence. Allocate approximately two minutes to conceptual grounding, four minutes to discrimination and justification, and two minutes to feedback. No persistent learner artefact is required.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Distinguish descriptive statements about statistical association from statements proposing or asserting causal relationships.","related_concepts":["Association","Causation","Causal language"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"},{"statement":"Explain why an observed correlation alone does not justify a claim about the effect of changing an economic variable.","related_concepts":["Observational evidence","Causal claims","Evidential limitations"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_1 modelled statistical interpretation using Datasets A and B. Commission comm_2 extended that capability through unfamiliar non-linear and unusual-observation examples. Learners should therefore bring an understanding of what a correlation coefficient describes and why examining the underlying observations matters. Revisit the household income and expenditure relationship from Dataset A so that the new intellectual demand concerns causal language and evidential justification rather than interpretation of unfamiliar data. The observations compare different households in the same month; they do not show the effect of an income intervention. Do not introduce worked explanations for the recurring advertising case. No individual learner response needs to be transferred into this component.

commissions.title: Exploring competing economic explanations
commissions.specification_text:
Create a nine-minute explanatory experience that establishes how different economic mechanisms and non-causal processes can produce observed statistical associations. Assume learners can interpret statistical relationships and distinguish associative statements from causal assertions. Use familiar Datasets A and B as grounding contexts, supplemented by brief explicitly hypothetical examples where necessary. Explain direct causal influence, reverse causality, common causes and confounding, shared trends and coincidental association. For each mechanism, make clear which variable could influence which other variable and why the proposed relationship could produce an observed association. For confounding, demonstrate why a plausible common cause must be capable of influencing both variables rather than merely being associated with one of them. Explain that several mechanisms may operate simultaneously and that a plausible economic account does not establish which mechanism actually generated the observations. Use simple relationship diagrams only where they clarify the explanation, accompanied by complete textual equivalents. Include brief guided reasoning checks that ask learners to discriminate between mechanisms, with explanatory feedback addressing causal direction and the role of common causes. Do not introduce formal causal graph notation, statistical adjustment or econometric estimation. Do not use the advertising case to supply worked alternative explanations that would pre-empt comm_5. Allocate approximately six minutes to explanation and contrasting examples, and three minutes to guided checks and feedback. No persistent learner-authored artefact is required.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Explain how direct causal influence, reverse causality and common causes can generate similar observed statistical associations.","related_concepts":["Economic mechanisms","Reverse causality","Confounding variables"],"cognitive_level":"understand"},{"statement":"Distinguish plausible causal mechanisms from non-causal sources of association, including shared trends and coincidence.","related_concepts":["Shared trends","Coincidental association","Observational ambiguity"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_3 established the distinction between describing an observed relationship and asserting a causal effect, using the household income and expenditure evidence from Dataset A. Learners now need conceptual resources for generating and explaining competing accounts of observed relationships. Reuse the established household and retailer-price contexts where appropriate, while keeping all proposed mechanisms explicitly hypothetical. Dataset B compares different retailers rather than the effects of changing a single retailer's price. The subsequent advertising case will require learners to generate their own alternative explanations, so this component must teach transferable explanatory principles without supplying the substantive answers to that case. No individual learner artefact needs to be transferred into this component.

commissions.title: Constructing alternative explanations for advertising and sales
commissions.specification_text:
Create an eight-minute practice experience requiring learners to generate their own economic explanations for a familiar statistical relationship. Revisit Dataset D and introduce the fictional claim that increasing a retailer's advertising expenditure will increase its sales revenue. Assume learners have already interpreted the dataset, distinguished association from causation and encountered modelled examples of direct causal influence, reverse causality, confounding and non-causal association. Display comm_2.E2 read-only as the learner's current earlier statistical interpretation. Provide the original evidence and a concise reasoning framework, but do not disclose the worked alternative explanations or supplementary evidence before the learner responds. Ask learners to distinguish the observed association from the causal claim, formulate at least two plausible competing explanations, explain how each could generate the observed relationship and identify why the available evidence cannot confidently distinguish between them. Declare elicitation_id E5 for a single coherent learner-authored response containing this reasoning. Capture the response as comm_5.E5. A compact response using short paragraphs or clearly connected explanatory points is appropriate to the time budget. After the learner has formulated a response, provide contrasting worked explanations and criterion-referenced formative feedback addressing economic plausibility, causal direction, whether a proposed common cause could influence both variables, and the limitations of observational evidence. Recognise that several defensible explanations are possible. Do not provide a confirmed explanation for R10 or imply that any proposed mechanism is established. Do not release the Case D supplement. Allocate approximately one minute to revisiting the evidence, four minutes to constructing explanations and three minutes to feedback. Retain the current learner-authored response for later reconsideration without claiming to preserve a separate pre-feedback version.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Construct plausible competing economic explanations for an observed relationship between advertising expenditure and sales revenue.","related_concepts":["Economic mechanisms","Reverse causality","Confounding"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"},{"statement":"Explain why the available observational evidence cannot confidently distinguish between competing causal accounts.","related_concepts":["Observational ambiguity","Evidential limitations","Causal claims"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_2 introduced Dataset D and asked learners to produce a statistical interpretation of the relationship between advertising expenditure and sales revenue, including the unusual observation R10. Commission comm_3 established the distinction between association and causal assertion. Commission comm_4 modelled competing explanatory mechanisms in other economic contexts. Bring forward comm_2.E2 as a declared read-only learner artefact so that learners can distinguish their own statistical description from the causal explanations they now generate. Preserve the ten retailer observations, units, identifiers and initial contextual limitations from the shared material. No confirmed reason for differences in advertising expenditure or sales revenue has been supplied. The Case D supplement must remain undisclosed until comm_8. The learner-authored explanations produced here will be displayed read-only in comm_8 and assembled into the Learning Journal. This component concludes week one.

commissions.title: Retrieving the foundations of causal reasoning
commissions.specification_text:
Create a five-minute retrieval practice experience opening the second week of the Learning Journey. Assume learners have previously interpreted statistical relationships, distinguished association from causation and constructed alternative economic explanations. Begin with retrieval before presenting explanatory reminders, worked examples or earlier learner responses. Use a small number of concise questions requiring learners to interpret a supplied correlation coefficient or compact economic evidence, discriminate between associative and causal statements, and distinguish plausible confounding from reverse causality. Use familiar concepts in brief, slightly varied hypothetical contexts rather than introducing a substantial new dataset or repeating the complete week-one explanations. Include immediate explanatory feedback that identifies the reasoning behind each answer and addresses likely misconceptions. Keep any numerical examples internally consistent and clearly synthetic. Do not release the advertising case supplement or introduce the final vocational training case. Do not introduce new conceptual content or require a written reflection. Allocate approximately three minutes to retrieval and two minutes to feedback. No persistent learner artefact is required.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Retrieve and apply the distinction between statistical association and causal influence when interpreting a brief economic example.","related_concepts":["Correlation","Association","Causation"],"cognitive_level":"apply"},{"statement":"Discriminate between confounding and reverse causality in a concise economic scenario.","related_concepts":["Confounding","Reverse causality","Causal direction"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: This component follows the interval between weeks one and two. Commission comm_1 established basic statistical interpretation; comm_2 explored non-linear relationships and unusual observations; comm_3 distinguished association from causation; comm_4 introduced competing explanatory mechanisms; and comm_5 required learners to construct their own explanations for advertising and sales. The educational purpose here is spaced retrieval of these capabilities before further evidential evaluation. Do not display comm_2.E2 or comm_5.E5 during the retrieval activity because doing so would supply reminders before learners attempt retrieval. No recurring scenario needs to be developed here. Preserve the advertising case for its planned reconsideration in comm_8.

commissions.title: Recognising evidence that strengthens causal explanations
commissions.specification_text:
Create a seven-minute explanatory experience that develops criteria for evaluating competing causal accounts. Assume learners can distinguish association from causation, generate plausible mechanisms and recognise confounding and reverse causality. Revisit familiar Dataset B, which compares product prices and weekly quantities sold across different retailers. Model why its observed negative association is consistent with a causal price effect but cannot establish that effect. Explain how additional information about temporal ordering, retailer characteristics, customer demand and meaningful comparisons could help distinguish explanations. Use clearly labelled hypothetical evidence conditions rather than adding fabricated observations to Dataset B. Contrast information that is merely consistent with an explanation with information that makes a competing explanation less plausible. Explain why temporal precedence is relevant but insufficient for establishing causation, and why comparisons between otherwise similar retailers can be informative without eliminating every possible source of confounding. Include brief guided judgements about which additional evidence would be more informative and why, followed by explanatory feedback. End with a compact evaluative framework that learners can apply to their own earlier explanations in the next component. Avoid formal causal identification techniques, regression, statistical adjustment and claims of definitive causal proof. Do not release the Case D supplement or introduce Dataset E. Allocate approximately four minutes to worked explanation and three minutes to guided evaluation and feedback. No persistent learner artefact is required.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Explain how temporal ordering and meaningful comparisons can strengthen or weaken competing causal explanations without necessarily establishing causation.","related_concepts":["Temporal ordering","Meaningful comparisons","Confounding"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"},{"statement":"Distinguish additional evidence that is merely consistent with a causal explanation from evidence that helps discriminate between competing explanations.","related_concepts":["Evidential discrimination","Alternative explanations","Residual uncertainty"],"cognitive_level":"evaluate"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_4 established how different mechanisms can generate similar associations. Commission comm_5 required learners to construct competing explanations for advertising and sales, and comm_6 retrieved the foundational concepts after the interval between weeks. Return to Dataset B from comm_1 as a familiar context for introducing a more demanding evidential question. The observations concern different retailers selling the same type of product during one week; they are not observations from a controlled price intervention. Any proposed additional evidence must be explicitly hypothetical and must not alter the locked observations. This component supplies evaluative criteria that learners will apply to their own advertising explanations in comm_8. Do not display or evaluate individual learner responses from comm_5 here.

commissions.title: Reconsidering the advertising and sales relationship
commissions.specification_text:
Create an eight-minute evidence-based revision practice experience. Learners revisit the familiar advertising and sales case from Dataset D and encounter previously unseen supplementary evidence from the shared authoritative material. Assume learners have constructed their own competing explanations and have subsequently learned how temporal ordering and meaningful comparisons can help evaluate those explanations. Display comm_5.E5 read-only as the learner's current earlier response. Present the original case information alongside the newly released preceding-month sales observations and budget-setting chronology. Ask learners to reconsider their earlier explanations, identifying what the supplementary evidence changes, which accounts become more or less plausible, which remain unresolved and how their conclusion should be qualified. Require explicit reference to relevant supplementary evidence rather than generic statements about correlation and causation. Declare elicitation_id E8 for a concise revised causal judgement and capture it as comm_8.E8. The revision itself is the learning performance; do not add a separate reflective task. After learners have formulated their revised judgement, provide worked reasoning and criterion-referenced feedback explaining why the timing of budget decisions and preceding-month sales figures make prior sales performance a relevant alternative explanation. Clarify that this evidence does not establish managers' actual motivations, eliminate a possible advertising effect, explain R10 or resolve unmeasured confounding. Allow defensible revisions that differ in their emphasis. Use exact shared observations, accessible tables and clear distinctions between established case facts and hypothetical mechanisms. Allocate approximately two minutes to reviewing the earlier response and supplementary evidence, four minutes to revision and two minutes to feedback. Do not claim to analyse the learner's earlier response automatically or generate personalised feedback based on its contents.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Reassess competing causal explanations for an economic relationship in light of additional evidence about temporal ordering and prior economic conditions.","related_concepts":["Temporal ordering","Reverse causality","Evidential discrimination"],"cognitive_level":"evaluate"},{"statement":"Revise a causal judgement to reflect what additional evidence strengthens, weakens or leaves unresolved.","related_concepts":["Revision of judgement","Evidential justification","Uncertainty"],"cognitive_level":"evaluate"}]}
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_END>>>
commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_2 introduced the advertising and sales dataset and elicited a statistical interpretation. Commission comm_5 asked learners to construct competing explanations for that relationship, including the possibility that the association does not establish the proposed advertising effect. Commission comm_7 introduced criteria for evaluating additional evidence. Display the declared artefact comm_5.E5 read-only so that learners can apply those criteria to their own earlier reasoning. Release the Case D supplement for the first time in this component. Preserve the exact preceding-month sales observations, the chronology of budget-setting decisions and all stated limitations. The new evidence concerns the same ten retailers, not a different sample or an experimental intervention. The learner's revised judgement comm_8.E8 will be included in the Learning Journal alongside the current earlier explanation. These are distinct learner-authored performances, not guaranteed historical snapshots of editable work.

commissions.title: Evaluating an unfamiliar economic policy claim
commissions.specification_text:
Create a fifteen-minute formative assessment experience whose principal educational job is to elicit interpretable evidence of integrated learner capability through independent transfer. Introduce Dataset E and the fictional policy claim that expanding vocational training participation will reduce local unemployment. This evidence and policy context must be first-pass unfamiliar. Assume learners have developed statistical interpretation skills, distinguished association from causation, constructed competing explanations and reconsidered a causal judgement using additional evidence. Provide the exact shared observations, a verified Pearson correlation coefficient, relevant contextual information and equivalent accessible graphical and tabular evidence. Ask learners to construct a coherent written evaluation suitable for a short evidence briefing to an economics policy audience. The response should describe the observed statistical relationship, distinguish the observed association from the policy claim, explain plausible competing accounts, evaluate what the available evidence supports, identify important uncertainties and propose additional evidence that would help distinguish explanations. Learners should recognise the limitations of area-level observational data without being required to use advanced statistical terminology or formal econometric techniques. Declare elicitation_id E9 for the complete learner-authored judgement and capture it as comm_9.E9. Provide concise assessment criteria covering statistical accuracy, distinction between association and causation, explanatory coherence, evidential justification and appropriate qualification. Criteria may describe the qualities of a strong response but must not reveal case-specific interpretations or substantive answers. Do not display earlier learner artefacts, worked solutions, preferred conclusions or detailed case-specific feedback during the independent performance. Detailed formative feedback is commissioned separately in comm_10. Any assessor-facing guidance must remain separate from the learner-facing task and must not be automatically exposed before the response opportunity. Allocate approximately three minutes to examining the evidence, ten minutes to constructing the judgement and two minutes to reviewing and recording the response. The assessment is formative and does not require automatic grading, AI evaluation or a formal summative mark. Keep the evidence set and response expectations proportionate to the allocated time.
<<<COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES_BEGIN>>>
{"learning_outcomes":[{"statement":"Interpret unfamiliar economic evidence accurately and distinguish the observed statistical relationship from a proposed policy effect.","related_concepts":["Statistical interpretation","Correlation","Causal policy claims"],"cognitive_level":"analyse"},{"statement":"Evaluate a causal economic claim by explaining plausible competing accounts and justifying an appropriately qualified conclusion using the available evidence.","related_concepts":["Confounding","Reverse causality","Economic mechanisms","Evidential justification"],"cognitive_level":"evaluate"},{"statement":"Identify additional evidence that would help discriminate between competing explanations of an observed economic relationship.","related_concepts":["Temporal ordering","Meaningful comparisons","Evidential limitations"],"cognitive_level":"evaluate"}]}

commissions.journey_context_text: Learners have progressed from interpreting statistical evidence in comm_1 and comm_2, through conceptual discrimination in comm_3, modelled causal explanations in comm_4, learner-generated explanations in comm_5, spaced retrieval in comm_6, evidential evaluation criteria in comm_7 and evidence-based revision in comm_8. Dataset E is a new context designed to test transfer rather than recall of the advertising case. It concerns ten fictional local labour market areas, vocational training participation and annual average unemployment rates. Preserve the exact sample definitions, observation pairs, units and contextual limitations. The observations are aggregated at area level and do not establish individual employment outcomes or the temporal sequence of individual training and employment changes. Do not reuse the advertising case or display earlier learner artefacts as scaffolding for this independent task. The resulting judgement comm_9.E9 will be displayed read-only in comm_10 and included in the Learning Journal. The separation of assessment and feedback is pedagogically intentional, but the runtime must not be described as preserving an immutable unaided or pre-feedback snapshot.

commissions.title: Refining and consolidating causal judgements
commissions.specification_text:
Create a ten-minute formative evaluation and refinement practice experience that follows the independent assessment in comm_9. Revisit the now-familiar vocational training and unemployment evidence from Dataset E. Display comm_9.E9 read-only as the learner's current assessment response. Provide a small set of contrasting worked judgements illustrating an unsupported causal assertion, an appropriately cautious but insufficiently justified conclusion, and a well-reasoned evaluation. Annotate the examples using the same substantive criteria established in comm_9: statistical accuracy, distinction between association and causation, explanatory coherence, consideration of competing accounts, evidential justification and appropriate qualification. Explain why particular reasoning moves improve or weaken a judgement rather than simply ranking the examples or revealing a preferred answer. Ask learners to apply these criteria to their own response, identify where their reasoning could be strengthened and produce a refined version of the substantive judgement. Declare elicitation_id E10 for the refined judgement and capture it as comm_10.E10. This must be a revision of the existing assessment performance, not a separate reflection or unrelated writing exercise. Learners whose existing reasoning is already strong should be able to improve precision, clarify evidential limitations or strengthen their proposal for additional evidence without being required to change a defensible conclusion. Feedback should acknowledge multiple plausible economic explanations while distinguishing hypotheses from established facts. Address the limitations of aggregated observational evidence and the absence of individual employment histories or established temporal ordering. Conclude with a concise transferable framework for evaluating future economic causal claims. Allocate approximately four minutes to comparing and evaluating worked judgements, two minutes to evaluating the learner's own response, three minutes to refinement and one minute to consolidation. Use the exact shared evidence and accessible representations. Do not claim automated assessment of the learner's response, personalised runtime feedback or preservation of immutable historical versions.

commissions.journey_context_text: Commission comm_9 presented the unfamiliar vocational training and unemployment case and required learners to formulate an independent written evaluation using the capabilities developed throughout the journey. Display the declared artefact comm_9.E9 read-only alongside the same locked evidence and assessment criteria. This component is the planned point at which worked case-specific evaluations and detailed formative feedback become available. The learner uses those examples and criteria to evaluate and refine their own substantive reasoning. Preserve all Dataset E facts and limitations; do not introduce new observations or assert that any particular causal mechanism is established. Capture the refined judgement separately as comm_10.E10. The Learning Journal will display the current versions of comm_9.E9 and comm_10.E10 as distinct developmental performances. Do not describe these as guaranteed pre-feedback and post-feedback snapshots. This component concludes week two and the complete Learning Journey.

continuity: The ten commissions realise the authoritative four-phase progression without changing any element or phase duration. Week one comprises comm_1 through comm_5, allocated 10 + 10 + 8 + 9 + 8 = 45 minutes. Week two comprises comm_6 through comm_10, allocated 5 + 7 + 8 + 15 + 10 = 45 minutes. Total authoritative allocation is exactly 90 minutes. The shared synthetic corpus provides factual continuity across independently generated products. Datasets A and B establish foundational interpretation and support later conceptual explanation. Dataset C exposes the limitations of linear correlation. Dataset D establishes a recurring advertising and sales case that develops from statistical interpretation in comm_2 to learner-generated causal explanations in comm_5 and evidence-based reconsideration in comm_8. Dataset E provides a genuinely unfamiliar transfer context in comm_9 and becomes familiar evidence for formative refinement in comm_10. The required learner-artefact handoffs are comm_2.E2 into comm_5, comm_5.E5 into comm_8, and comm_9.E9 into comm_10. Each handoff displays the declared learner-authored artefact read-only within the designated later component. No arbitrary stored responses, authoring-time inspection of published resources or response-aware adaptation are assumed. The five declared producer artefacts also populate the journey-level Learning Journal. The interval between weeks is used for spaced retrieval before earlier responses are revisited. Independent assessment is separated from detailed case-specific feedback to preserve the intended opportunity for transfer, without asserting that the runtime guarantees immutable response histories. Expository commissions own conceptual grounding and worked explanation; practice commissions own discrimination, application, retrieval, revision and formative improvement; the assessment pack owns elicitation of integrated evidence of capability. A separate situated task is not commissioned because authentic economic reasoning is already embedded within the practice and assessment experiences, and an additional contextual task would duplicate educational functions or exceed the available time. All required educational jobs are represented by supported product types.

journal.decision_basis: The Learning Journal is justified by both functional continuity and developmental visibility. Learners naturally produce five meaningful text artefacts while interpreting evidence, constructing explanations, reconsidering those explanations and evaluating an unfamiliar causal claim. Three declared handoffs support purposeful reuse of earlier reasoning within later components. Assembling all five artefacts into a lightweight read-only Journal enables learners to examine how their statistical descriptions develop into increasingly justified and appropriately qualified causal judgements. The Journal does not require additional writing, separate reflection, mandatory completion or an additional product commission. Entries display the current learner-authored work available from the declared producer components rather than immutable historical versions.
journal.title: Learning Journal: From correlation to causal judgement

entries.title: Interpreting advertising and sales data
entries.framing: Your statistical description of the advertising and sales relationship, including the overall pattern and unusual observation. This provides a foundation for distinguishing what the data show from possible explanations.

entries.title: Competing explanations for advertising and sales
entries.framing: Your account of plausible mechanisms that could produce the observed relationship and the reasons why the available evidence cannot confidently distinguish between them.

entries.title: Reconsidering explanations using additional evidence
entries.framing: Your revised judgement about advertising and sales in light of additional evidence. Consider how the evidential justification and treatment of uncertainty relate to your earlier explanation.

entries.title: Evaluating a vocational training policy claim
entries.framing: Your assessment response applying statistical interpretation and causal reasoning to the relationship between vocational training participation and local unemployment.

entries.title: Refining an economic causal judgement
entries.framing: Your refined evaluation of the vocational training policy claim, informed by worked examples and criteria for defensible economic reasoning.

feasibility_note: The authoritative 90-minute budget is preserved exactly, including explanation, evidence interpretation, learner-authored responses, feedback and revision. The breadth of the intended learning makes this a tightly bounded introductory journey rather than a comprehensive treatment of causal inference. Downstream generation must avoid expanding the number of examples, duplicating explanations or adding substantial reading and reflection requirements. The assessment and revision commissions are feasible only with compact evidence sets, concise response expectations and focused feedback. The selection of ten commissions, their product assignments, the synthetic economic contexts, the shared corpus and the three artefact handoffs are commissioning decisions made within the supplied educational requirements. The raw synthetic observations are locked at this stage, but derived correlation coefficients other than the mathematically symmetric zero-correlation example have not been independently calculated or verified in this capture; downstream generation must calculate and validate them before publication. Graphical and tabular representations must use identical observations. Runtime implementation must verify that each declared elicitation produces the intended persistent text artefact, that the assessment pack can expose comm_9.E9 for subsequent read-only reuse, and that detailed assessment feedback is not presented prematurely. If these capabilities are unavailable, preserve the affected educational requirements and Journal entries explicitly rather than silently substituting recognition questions or omitting learner-authored reasoning. The Journal displays current editable learner work and cannot guarantee preservation of immutable pre-feedback or unaided versions. Consequently, developmental visibility is supported through distinct performances and purposeful revisions, not through a verified historical audit trail. The proposed internal activity timings are design estimates within the authoritative commission allocations and should be checked through learner testing.
